name: Sam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on building sites fitting kitchens, partitions and the odd window frame that arrived the wrong size. I have a vocational trade certificate and enough site time to know how to make a good joint, though I am an ordinary worker rather than a foreman. I use AI now and then to clean up a materials list, but I still mark the actual wall with a pencil. My partner Rina and I have two school-age children, a mortgage, higher pay for the trade, and about ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other building firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site team that a neater materials list is welcome, but the carpenter still measures the opening. A pencil mark on plaster is more useful than a perfect drawing of the wrong wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work and pay would keep moving as usual, and our savings make this a small change at home. I would keep the tool only if the merchant sends the right materials from its list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my kitchen-fitting rota and check the AI materials list against site measurements. In the first year I would compare three orders with what actually arrived before changing my usual ordering method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have a mortgage, but nothing here suggests my paid work is going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wrong order wastes the most time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cabinet panel that is ten millimetres too wide leaves the kitchen half finished until the replacement arrives. I would write the actual opening on the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another AI subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already use a company tool occasionally; the family has better uses for our money than a second list maker.

say: **Material lists** help only after a carpenter measures each kitchen opening on the actual building site.
**Carpentry fitting** still depends on the real wall.
think: My **work and pay** stay steady under the plateau.
Ten months saved give our **household** a strong buffer.
do: **Stay** on the kitchen-fitting rota and check materials against wall measurements.
**Compare** three AI orders with delivered panels before changing the method.
feel: **Calm** about paid work and the mortgage.
S0.quote: A pencil mark on plaster is more useful than a perfect drawing of the wrong wall.
fieldNote: He uses **AI occasionally** for lists but judges orders by what arrives on site.
His **higher pay and savings** make a small software change financially secure.

steps.text: Keep kitchen-fitting rota with measured material orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the buying and booking office changes before anyone has a robot fit cabinets on a building site. I would test new delivery schedules on real kitchens before accepting a shorter job allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If materials arrive correctly, I could finish earlier and still earn my wage. If the office cuts too many checkers, wrong panels might leave a crew waiting, but I do not expect my own income to fall soon with many local firms hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log five cabinet jobs, noting delivery time, wrong panels and the hours spent fitting. During the first year I would show the record to the site manager and agree to a new target only where the materials and time match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a rush to trust the schedule, secure about my pay. I have seen enough missing hinges to want a real cabinet delivery trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which job would you use as an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small kitchen at the back of a site often has the least space to store a wrong cabinet. I would record both the delivery delay and the second trip to fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another employer now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the better-paying job I have and see whether the five-job trial supports the new schedule.

say: **Buying and booking** change before robots can fit cabinets and partitions on a building site.
**Delivery trials** should precede shorter job allowances.
think: Wrong panels may waste hours, but my **own wage** looks secure nearby.
do: **Log** deliveries and fitting hours on five cabinet jobs.
**Accept** shorter targets only where material and time records match.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed targets, secure about income.
S1.quote: I have seen enough missing hinges to want a real cabinet delivery trial.
fieldNote: He is **open to change** after a small trial rather than an abstract promise.
He expects **personal pay security** given current higher wages and many nearby firms.

steps.text: Keep current kitchen job while testing five delivery schedules
Wait for five-job records before accepting shorter targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my workmates that thinking AI could handle buying and plans by 2028, while robots that can fit kitchens as well as people arrive around 2031. We still have the physical work in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose well-paid fitting shifts after 2031, even if a robot cannot reach every odd corner. We have ten months saved and nearby firms, but I cannot assume their new jobs will pay what my current site does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put one tenth of each new pay cheque into a separate savings account starting this month, while keeping the mortgage current. If the contractor funds training for a posted local site-measuring role with a wage that covers our bills, I would take the course; after 2028 I would apply for that role, and keep kitchen shifts until an offer is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a good wage, but not cornered. I have time to add to the buffer and inspect real openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new savings cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would build another few months of household expenses, not buy a machine I have never used. If the mortgage payment rose, Rina and I would revisit the tenth before missing a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the site-measuring role pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted wage with mortgage, school and food bills. A title with a short monthly cheque would not be an improvement over fitting kitchens.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches buying before capable kitchen-fitting robots around 2031.
**Physical fitting** remains work during the gap.
think: Robots could cut my **higher-paid shifts** after 2031.
Our **ten-month reserve** and nearby firms help, but equal wages are uncertain.
do: **Save** one tenth of new site pay while mortgage bills allow.
**Take** funded measuring course for posted local bill-covering role.
**Apply** after 2028 for that role, keeping fitting shifts until offered.
feel: **Anxious** about wage replacement, with room to act.
S2.quote: A title with a short monthly cheque would not be an improvement over fitting kitchens.
fieldNote: His **new saving** comes from future pay, separate from the reserve already held.
His **course and application** require employer funding, a posted local role and wages covering regular bills.

steps.text: Save one tenth of new site pay while mortgage bills allow
Take funded measuring course for posted local bill-covering role
Apply after 2028 for posted local measuring role if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives employers room to test building robots on crooked kitchens before thinking AI arrives in 2031. The robots reach full hands-on ability around 2034, and I would rather watch real site work than a smooth demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but the mortgage may not be gone. If fitting work thins out in 2034, I would want a job that uses my measurements and pays enough, not a new label with less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting kitchens and take a paid site-measurement course if my contractor offers it with a real local vacancy. In the first year after 2031 I would apply for the posted measuring job only if its wage covers our household bills; otherwise I would stay on paid fitting shifts while they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, with a longer runway than the fast picture. I can learn a proved site-measuring method, but I will not trade my kitchen-fitting wage for a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the robot fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch it scribe a cabinet side against a wall that bows at the floor. The panel should meet the plaster without a gap you can see from the doorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course if the contractor would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted local job required it and the wage made the cost recoverable. I would not spend the family buffer on a speculative qualification.

say: **Crooked-kitchen trials** should precede capable site robots around 2034, before contractors cut carpentry crews.
**Actual site fit** matters more than a smooth demonstration.
think: The **mortgage** may still require strong pay in 2034.
A **measuring role** is useful only with a bill-covering wage.
do: **Take** paid measuring course if contractor offers real local vacancy.
**Apply** after 2031 only for posted bill-covering measuring job.
**Keep** fitting shifts if no offer arrives.
feel: **Wary**, but able to learn a proven method.
S3.quote: I can learn a proved site-measuring method, but I will not trade my kitchen-fitting wage for a brochure.
fieldNote: His **course condition** needs a real vacancy and paid time, or a posted wage that recovers self-funded costs.
His **application** preserves local vacancy and bill-covering pay, while fitting remains the fallback.

steps.text: Take contractor-paid measuring course if real local vacancy offered
Apply after 2031 for posted local measuring job only if pay covers bills
Keep kitchen-fitting shifts if no local offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and fully capable site robots around 2039. I would use the time to pay more off the mortgage and show my children how to fit a joint with a square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties when the robots arrive, so I cannot treat this as a retirement question. Our savings make room to plan, yet the better-paid kitchen jobs could still be fewer by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the site work and put an extra fixed amount toward the mortgage from each pay cheque if our ordinary bills stay covered. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for local building-measurement work only if a genuine post pays enough for the household and any required course is funded or affordable from new earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the far end, but I can make the debt smaller before the machines reach my tools. I would rather teach my children a carpentry joint and a household budget together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina and I could try fifty from each pay cheque after the usual bills. We would pause the extra payment if school costs rose, without touching the ten-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them why a square tells the truth about a cabinet corner. I would also show how we keep the mortgage payment ahead of optional spending.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable site robots around 2039.
**Trade skills** and household budgets both matter to his children.
think: Better-paid **kitchen-fitting shifts** could be fewer by 2039, when capable site robots reach physical work.
Our **savings** buy time to lower the mortgage.
do: **Keep** fitting kitchens on the current site.
**Pay** fifty extra on mortgage from each cheque if ordinary bills stay covered.
**Apply** after 2036 for local measuring only with real bill-covering post and funded or affordable course.
feel: **Anxious** about later wages, with time to lower debt.
S4.quote: I would rather teach my children a carpentry joint and a household budget together.
fieldNote: He commits **new pay** to extra mortgage payments, conditional on ordinary bills.
His **later job move** needs a genuine local post, bill-covering wages and funded or affordable training.

steps.text: Keep kitchen-fitting shifts on current site
Pay fifty extra on mortgage from each pay cheque if bills stay covered
Apply after 2036 for posted local bill-covering measuring job with funded or affordable course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because kitchen-fitting robots around 2031 could cut well-paid shifts while my children still depend on the mortgage being paid. A funded measuring course attached to a posted local job would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a perfectly cut cabinet meets a wall that leans. I want the person with the pencil to decide whether the cabinet fit is good before anyone signs the job off.

portrait: **Sam Haddad**, 43, is an experienced construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits kitchens and partitions.
He and partner Rina have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, higher trade pay and about ten months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for materials lists, adopting a new schedule only after real delivery trials prove it.
In **AGI by 2028**, he saves new pay and considers a funded measuring course for a posted bill-covering local role.
A **decade-long runway** lets him make extra mortgage payments from wages while continuing site work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut higher-paid kitchen shifts around 2031 while mortgage and school bills continue.
whatWouldHelp: A funded **measuring course** attached to a posted local bill-covering job would protect household pay.
headlineQuote: I want the person with the pencil to decide whether the cabinet fit is good before anyone signs the job off.
